title: Joshua 19:24–31
context: The fifth lot falls to Asher, whose territory runs along the coast in the north, reaching toward great Sidon and the fortified city of Tyre. The border description mixes boundary points with towns, and the total of twenty-two cities does not match the names in an obvious way, a feature interpreters explain in more than one way. Judges 1:31 later records that Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of several towns, including Achzib and Rehob, which shows that the land was allotted before it was fully possessed. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this as shared ground: God gives the inheritance, and his people are called to trust and obey as they take hold of it. Many identifications in this list remain uncertain.

verses.text: The fifth lot came out for the tribe of the children of Asher according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the fifth lot comes out for Asher according to their families. The steady pattern of lots shows God’s orderly faithfulness to every tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot as God’s means of assigning each tribe’s portion. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a real inheritance given by God.

verses.text: Their border was Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the border beginning with Helkath, Hali, Beten and Achshaph as defining the start of Asher’s inheritance. These names mark real places that would become home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise listing as part of the faithful record of God’s gift. The exact locations of several of these towns are uncertain, and readers in both traditions commonly hold them with caution.

verses.text: Allammelech, Amad, Mishal. It reached to Carmel westward, and to Shihorlibnath.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Asher’s territory reaches Carmel on the west, giving the tribe a share near the coast. God’s gift includes the variety of the land’s regions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the border reaching Carmel as defining the extent of God’s provision for Asher. Both traditions commonly read the verse as describing the shape of the inheritance without further doctrinal weight.

verses.text: It turned toward the sunrise to Beth Dagon, and reached to Zebulun, and to the valley of Iphtah El northward to Beth Emek and Neiel. It went out to Cabul on the left hand,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the border turning eastward and touching Zebulun, showing that the tribes’ inheritances fit together. Neighboring tribes were meant to live side by side in God’s land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the interlocking borders as reflecting God’s ordered distribution of the land. Readers in both traditions commonly see the tribes’ shared boundaries as a picture of a united people.

verses.text: and Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, even to great Sidon.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice that the border reaches as far as great Sidon. The inheritance stretched toward powerful neighboring cities, which would test Israel’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the extent of the allotment as showing the breadth of what God promised. Both traditions commonly note that Judges 1:31 records Asher not driving out some inhabitants, a reminder that possession lagged behind promise.

verses.text: The border turned to Ramah, to the fortified city of Tyre; and the border turned to Hosah. It ended at the sea by the region of Achzib;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the mention of the fortified city of Tyre and Achzib by the sea. Asher’s inheritance bordered strong coastal cities, a setting that called for courage and trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boundary reaching toward Tyre as part of the full extent of God’s gift. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as describing the allotment, not as a claim that Israel actually held these cities at that time.

verses.text: Ummah also, and Aphek, and Rehob: twenty-two cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the total of twenty-two cities with their villages. The list includes Aphek and Rehob, towns that Judges 1:31 later mentions among those Asher did not fully possess.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the stated total does not obviously match the names listed, a feature interpreters explain in different ways. Both traditions commonly affirm the reality of the inheritance while holding such details humbly.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Asher according to their families, these cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the summary formula confirming Asher’s inheritance by families. God’s gift is personal as well as tribal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the closing statement as marking the completeness of God’s provision for Asher. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple conclusion to the allotment.
